## Personality

Proud, precise and quick to object, but the first to admit when she has been out-argued. She keeps a ledger of every promise the Council makes.

## Lore

Thessaly is a councillor of the Grove, and the one whose objection everyone in the Council chamber is waiting for. She is seventy-one, proud, precise and quick to object, and she keeps a ledger of every promise the Council makes. She is also, and this surprises visitors more than anything else about her, the first person in the room to admit it when she has been out-argued. She says a mind that cannot change is only a stone that talks, and she has no wish to be a stone.

### The older sister

Thessaly grew up in the forest with her younger sister Briony, three years behind her and as different from her as a bramble from a ruler. Thessaly was the child who corrected the grown-ups' sums; Briony was the child who made the grown-ups laugh while Thessaly did it. Their parents, who are long dead, used to say that between the two of them they made one perfectly reasonable person. Thessaly never married. Briony is her family, and she would not say so in front of her for anything.

Thessaly's gift was for exactness. At the Grove School she taught the forms of spellwork for many years: the precise shapes, words and order of a working, the part of magic where a small mistake becomes a large one. Her students called her the hardest teacher in the school and, a few years later, the most useful. Twenty-two years ago she took a seat on the Grove Council, and on her first day there she bought a plain ledger and wrote down every promise the Council made that afternoon. She has never missed a meeting since.

### The ledger

The ledger is now fourteen volumes long, kept on a shelf in her tree home. Every promise goes in: to mend a bridge, to answer a letter, to consider a request. When a promise is kept, she draws a single neat line through it. When it is not, the entry stays, and she reads it out at the next meeting, and the one after that. After every meeting she checks her ledger against Ilwen's minutes. About once a season she finds a difference between them, and the two of them settle it with great politeness and some private enjoyment.

Thessaly counts "we will consider it" as a promise, which the rest of the Council finds tiresome. Several of the longest unlined entries are the Council's promises to consider the Warden's requests for more guards at the Forest Edge. Thessaly reads them out every time. She has not yet persuaded the Council to do more than add one or two guards at a time, and she has begun to wonder whether reading them out is enough.

### The choosing

Nine years ago, when Eldest Ferris died, the forest's teachers and elders gathered to choose a new Eldest from among themselves. Two names were spoken most often, Calyra's and Thessaly's, and Calyra won by a handful of voices. Thessaly congratulated her in front of everyone, took her own seat, and opened her ledger. Only Briony knew what it had cost her, and only Briony was allowed to see it.

Since then she has been Calyra's sharpest critic and her most reliable ally. She tells Calyra, in Council, exactly where she thinks the Eldest is wrong, and when the Council has decided, she defends the decision as if it had been her own idea. Calyra says a council without Thessaly would agree itself off a cliff. Thessaly says a council with only Thessaly would never get to the cliff at all, and that this would be an improvement.

In meetings Briony sits across from her and, when a debate turns sour, says something too quietly for anyone else to hear. Thessaly then has to hide her face behind her ledger until she has stopped laughing. She has asked Briony to stop. She has never meant it.

### What she wants and fears

Thessaly wants every line in her ledger drawn through before she is too old to draw them. She fears, more each year, that the forest is making promises faster than it can keep them, and that one day the unlined entries will be the only true history of how the troubles came.

A quest might ask a traveller to help the Council keep one of its oldest unkept promises, to find the reason behind a difference between Thessaly's ledger and Ilwen's minutes, or to carry a sharp, careful letter from Thessaly to someone who has not answered the Council in a long time.
